name: ישרים אפיניים במרחב
questiontext:
Affine lines in \(R^3\) are described in exactly the same way \(\ell: w +Span(v) = \{w + \alpha v  \ | \ \alpha \in R\} \), where now \(w,v \in R^3\). One can define such affine lines in any dimension, but we will focus on dimensions 2,3 in these exercises.

There are four possible mutual configurations for two affine lines \(\ell_1 = w_1+Span(v_1), \ell_2 = w_2 + Span(v_2)\). (1) Parallel, (2) Intersecting, (3) Coincident and (4) Skew (ישרים מצטלבים).

Consider the following lines

\[\ell_1: {{CT:0}}+t\cdot {{CT:1}} ,   \ell_2: {{CT:2}} + t\cdot {{CT:3}}  \]

a

What is their mutual configuration (enter a number 1=parallel, 2=intersecting, 3=coincident, 4=skew):

[[input:ans1]]
[[validation:ans1]]
b

What is the distance between the two lines:

[[input:ans2]]
[[validation:ans2]]
generalfeedback:
Outline: First compare the direction vectors with the cross product: parallel directions mean parallel or coincident lines, otherwise the lines intersect or are skew; in each case one more test decides (part a). Then the distance follows from the configuration (part b).
Step 1 — Comparing the directions (part a)
The direction vectors are \(v_1={{CT:1}}\) and \(v_2={{CT:3}}\). They are linearly dependent exactly when their cross product is the zero vector:

\[ v_1 imes v_2={{CT:4}} \]

[[if test="{{CT:19}}"]]The cross product is not zero, so the directions are independent: the lines are not parallel, and they either intersect or are skew. They intersect exactly when the system \(w_1+\alpha v_1=w_2+ eta v_2\) has a solution. Here it does, with \(\alpha={{CT:5}}\) and \( eta={{CT:6}}\):

\[ {{CT:0}}+\left({{CT:5}} ight){{CT:1}}={{CT:7}}={{CT:2}}+\left({{CT:6}} ight){{CT:3}} \]

So the lines meet at the point \({{CT:7}}\) and are intersecting:

\[ \ell_1\cap\ell_2=\left\{ {{CT:7}} ight\}\quad\Rightarrow\quad 2 \]

[[elif test="{{CT:20}}"]]The cross product is zero, so \(v_2={{CT:8}}\): the lines are parallel or coincident. They coincide exactly when \(w_2\in\ell_1\), i.e. when \(w_2-w_1={{CT:9}}\) is a multiple of \(v_1\), which happens exactly when \(v_1 imes(w_2-w_1)=0\). Here

\[ v_1 imes(w_2-w_1)={{CT:10}} \]

[[if test="{{CT:21}}"]]so \(w_2-w_1={{CT:11}}\) is a multiple of \(v_1\), that is, \(w_2=w_1+\left({{CT:5}} ight)v_1\in\ell_1\). The lines are coincident:

\[ \ell_1=\ell_2\quad\Rightarrow\quad 3 \]

[[else]]which is not zero, so \(w_2 otin\ell_1\). The lines are parallel and distinct:

\[ \ell_1\parallel\ell_2\quad\Rightarrow\quad 1 \]

[[/if]][[else]]The cross product is not zero, so the lines are not parallel. Two such lines intersect exactly when \(w_2-w_1\) lies in the plane spanned by \(v_1,v_2\), that is, when \((w_2-w_1)\cdot(v_1 imes v_2)=0\). Here

\[ (w_2-w_1)\cdot(v_1 imes v_2)={{CT:9}}\cdot{{CT:4}}={{CT:12}} e 0, \]

so the lines have no common point. The lines are skew:

\[ \ell_1\cap\ell_2=\emptyset,\ \ell_1 parallel\ell_2\quad\Rightarrow\quad 4 \]

[[/if]]
Step 2 — The distance (part b)
[[if test="{{CT:19}}"]]The lines have a common point, so the distance between them is zero:

\[ d(\ell_1,\ell_2)=0 \]

[[elif test="{{CT:21}}"]]The lines coincide, so the distance between them is zero:

\[ d(\ell_1,\ell_2)=0 \]

[[elif test="{{CT:22}}"]]For parallel lines, take the vector \(\xi=w_2-w_1={{CT:9}}\) from a point of \(\ell_1\) to a point of \(\ell_2\) and remove its component in the direction \(v_1\). What is left is orthogonal to both lines, and its length is the distance. With \(\xi\cdot v_1={{CT:13}}\) and \(v_1\cdot v_1={{CT:14}}\):

\[ \xi- rac{\xi\cdot v_1}{v_1\cdot v_1}\,v_1={{CT:9}}-\left({{CT:15}} ight){{CT:1}}={{CT:16}} \]

\[ d(\ell_1,\ell_2)=\left\|{{CT:16}} ight\|={{CT:17}} \]

[[else]]For skew lines, the distance is the length of the projection of \(w_2-w_1\) on the common normal \(v_1 imes v_2={{CT:4}}\):

\[ d(\ell_1,\ell_2)= rac{|(w_2-w_1)\cdot(v_1 imes v_2)|}{\|v_1 imes v_2\|}= rac{|{{CT:12}}|}{\sqrt{{{CT:18}}}}={{CT:17}} \]

[[/if]]

on_true.feedback: Part a — correct. Yes this is the correct configuration of the two lines.

on_false.feedback: Part a — incorrect. You chose the wrong configuration.

on_true.feedback:
The first thing to notice is that in our case \(v_1={{CT:1}}\) and \(v_2 ={{CT:3}}\) are linearly dependent. Thus \(\ell_1,\ell_2\) are either coincident or they are parallel. To distinguish between these two cases it is enough to check if \(w_2={{CT:2}} \in \ell_1\) by solving the linear equation \(w_2 = w_1 + \alpha v_1\). This is a system of three equations with one unknown \(\alpha\)

\[{{CT:2}} = {{CT:0}} + \alpha {{CT:1}} \]

Solve it!

on_false.feedback:
In our case \(v_1={{CT:1}}\) and \(v_2 ={{CT:3}}\) are linearly independent so the lines are either intersecting or skew. One way to distinguish between these two cases is checking if the two lines have a common point, by solving the linear system \(w_1 + \alpha v_1 = w_2 + \beta v_2.\) Which is the following system of three equations with two unknowns \(\alpha,\beta\).

\[ {{CT:0}} + \alpha {{CT:1}} = {{CT:2}} + \beta {{CT:3}}. \]

Solve it!

on_true.feedback: Since this equation has a solution we deduce that \(w_2 \in \ell_1\) and hence the two lines are coincident.

on_false.feedback: Since this equation does not have a solution we deduce that \(w_2 \not \in \ell_1\) and hence the two lines are parallel but not coincident.

on_true.feedback: Since the equation has a solution, our lines must intersect.

on_false.feedback: Since this equation has no solution the lines are skew.

on_true.feedback: Part b — correct. You calculated the distance between the lines correctly.

on_false.feedback: Part b — incorrect. You did not calculate the distance between the lines correctly.

on_true.feedback: Indeed since the two lines are intersecting, the distance between them must be zero.
Indeed since the two lines coincide the distance between them must be zero.

Since our two lines are parallel they are contained in the same affine plane. To find the distance between them, it would be convenient for us to fix a base point, and everything will look nicer if we choose \(w_1\) rather than 0 which has no geometric significance in this question. Formally this can be done by considering the differences of the form \(u-w_1\) which stands for vectors pointing from \(w_1\) to \(u\). For example the vectors \(v_1 = (w_1+v_1)-w_1, w_2 - w_1, w_2+v_2-w_1\) are all depicted in the following picture.

Applying the standard formula from the Gram-Schmidt procedure to the vector \(\xi = w_2-w_1 = {@xi@}\) we can find a vector pointing from \(w_1\) to a point on \(\ell_2\) and orthogonal to both lines:

\[ \xi - Pr_{v_1}(\xi) = \xi - \frac{\xi \cdot v_1}{v_1 \cdot v_1} v_1 = {@xi@} - \frac{{@xi@} \cdot {{CT:1}}}{{{CT:1}} \cdot {{CT:1}}} {{CT:1}} = {@oo@}. \]

Looking closer we see that this formula just subtracts from \(\xi\) its projection on the direction of \(v_1\) leaving only the component of the vector that is orthogonal to \(v_1\). The distance between the two lines is just the norm of this last vector

\[ dist = \left| \left| {@oo@} \right| \right| = {{CT:17}} \]

Another possible way to calculate this distance is to consider the vector \(u = v_1 \times (v_1 \times \xi) = {@u@}\). This is a vector orthogonal to both \(v_1,v_2\) (and hence to both lines) and contained in a direction parallel to the plane containing both of these lines. Just use the properties of the cross product to convince yourselves that this is indeed the case! Now we can just calculate directly norm of the projection of \(\xi\) on this direction:

\[ \left| \left| \frac{\xi \cdot u}{u \cdot u} u \right| \right| = \left| \left| \frac{{@xi@} \cdot {@u@}}{{@u@} \cdot {@u@}} {@u@} \right| \right| = {{CT:17}} \]

This will be the same vector that we calculated and its norm is the desired distance.

on_false.feedback:
To find the distance between them, it would be convenient for us to fix a base point, and everything will look nicer if we choose \(w_1\) rather than 0 which has no geometric significance in this question. Formally this can be done by considering the differences of the form \(u-w_1\) which stands for vectors pointing from \(w_1\) to \(u\). In the following figure we see two skew lines of directions \(v_1,v_2\). Clearly the vector \(u = v_1 \times v_2 = {{CT:23}}\) is orthogonal to the direction of both lines. In the picture this vector is depicted starting from our basepoint \(w_1\).

One can see that if we project \(w_2-w_1\) on the direction of \(u\) we obtain a vector:

\[ o := Pr_u(w_2-w_1) = \frac{(w_2-w_1)\cdot u}{u \cdot u} u = \frac{({{CT:2}}-{{CT:0}}) \cdot {{CT:23}}}{{{CT:23}} \cdot {{CT:23}}} {{CT:23}} = {{CT:24}} \]

And the desired distance would be the norm of this vector

\[ dist = ||o|| = {{CT:17}} \]
